Definition: Integers
The numbers −1, −2, −3, … (to the left of zero) are negative numbers or negative integers, and the numbers 1, 2, 3, … (to the right of zero) are positive numbers or positive integers.
Hence, the new set of numbers …, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3,… are called integers.

The Elevator Story:
Imagine you're in a tall building with an elevator. This is one of the best ways to understand positive and negative integers:
Ground floor = 0
(our starting point)
Floors above ground = Positive integers
(+1, +2, +3...)
Basement floors = Negative integers

When the elevator goes up from the ground floor, you're moving to positive floors. When it goes below ground level, you enter the negative floors.(basements).

CISCE: Class 6
Introduction
Ordering integers means arranging numbers based on their size. A number line is a useful tool for visually comparing and ordering integers.
Numbers on the right side of a number line are greater than numbers on the left side.
Numbers on the left side of a number line are smaller than those on the right.
5 is to the right of 2, meaning 5 > 2.
0 is to the right of -3, meaning 0 > -3.
2 is to the right of -1, meaning 2 > -1.
-4 is to the left of -3, meaning -4 < -3.
-3 is to the left of 4, meaning -3 < 4.
CISCE: Class 6
Properties of Integer Ordering
Every positive integer is greater than 0.
Every positive integer is greater than every negative integer.
Zero is greater than every negative integer but smaller than every positive integer.
Every negative integer is smaller than every positive integer.

Introduction
Triangle construction is the process of accurately drawing a triangle using basic geometric tools—a ruler (straightedge), a compass, and often a protractor—when given specific measurements. These measurements are typically side lengths or angle measures.
CISCE: Class 6
Construction 1: Three Sides Given (SSS)
Example:
Construct triangle ABC with
AB = 7.6 cm
AC = 6 cm
CB = 4 cm
Steps:
Draw a rough sketch of triangle ABC.
Draw the base AB = 7.6 cm.
With A as center, draw an arc of radius 6 cm.
With B as center, draw another arc of radius 4 cm. Let the arcs intersect at point C.
Join AC and BC.
CISCE: Class 6
Construction 2: Two Sides and Included Angle Given (SAS)
Example:
Construct triangle ABC with
AB = 3 cm
BC = 5 cm
∠ABC = 60°
Steps:
Draw a rough sketch of triangle ABC.
Draw base BC = 5 cm.
At point B, use a protractor to construct ∠ABC = 60°.
With B as the centre, draw an arc of radius 3 cm to locate point A on the 60° line.
Join AC.
CISCE: Class 6
Construction 3: Two Angles and the Included Side Given (ASA)
Example:
Construct triangle ABC with
AB = 4 cm
∠A = 60°
∠B = 30°
Steps:
Draw a rough sketch of triangle ABC.
Draw the base AB = 4 cm.
At point A, draw a 60° angle (ray AP).

Definition: Natural Numbers
Natural numbers are the numbers used for counting, beginning from 1 onwards.
They are denoted by the set
N
= {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, …}
Maharashtra State Board: Class 6
Characteristics of Natural Numbers
The first and the smallest natural number is 1 (one).
It is impossible to obtain the last and greatest natural number. [In fact, there are infinite natural numbers, like counting the stars in nature.]
The difference between any two consecutive natural numbers is 1 (one).
By adding 1 to any natural number, its next natural number is obtained.
The fractions, like
`3/4
, – `12/17`, `215/317` etc., are not natural numbers.
The decimal numbers like 3.4, 5.28, 2.227, etc., are not natural.
0 (zero) is not a natural number.
No natural number is negative; i.e., none of -15, -3, -214, etc., is a natural number.
If n is any natural number
(i) 2n is an even natural number and
(ii) (2n - 1) is an odd natural number.
CISCE: Class 6
Real-Life Examples
Counting pencils in a box: Natural numbers: 1, 2, 3,…
Taking attendance: “Present: 35 students”—that’s a natural number.
Scoring points in a game, numbering pages in a book, or steps climbed — all use natural numbers.
CISCE: Class 6
Key Points Summary
Natural numbers:
Counting numbers from 1 onwards (
N = {1, 2, 3, …}).
No zeros, no negatives, no decimals or fractions—only
whole counts.
Each natural number has a unique successor: just add 1.

Definition: Whole numbers
Whole numbers
are a foundational concept in mathematics, encompassing all non-negative integers starting from zero.
Example: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ..., 367, 368, ..., 237105, ...
CISCE: Class 6
Characteristic of Whole Numbers
A whole number is either 0 or a natural number.
The first and the smallest whole number is 0 (zero).
It is impossible to obtain the last and greatest whole number. [Like natural numbers, whole numbers are also infinite].
The difference between two consecutive whole numbers is 1 (one).
By adding 1 to any whole number, its next whole number is obtained.
All natural numbers are whole numbers; not all whole numbers are natural numbers.
The number line used to represent whole numbers is as given below:
Zero (0) is the smallest whole number.
There is no whole number on the left side of 0.
Each whole number (apart from 0) is on the right side of 0.
A whole number is
(a) greater than every whole number on its left.
(b) smaller than every whole number on its right.

Addition of Algebraic Expressions:
1. Addition of like terms:
If we have to add like terms then we can simply add their numerical coefficients.
The sum of two or more like terms is a like term with a numerical coefficient equal to the sum of the numerical coefficients of all the like terms.
Example: 6x + 5x = (6 + 5)x = 11x.
2. Addition of unlike terms:
If we have to add the unlike terms then we just have to put an addition sign between the terms.
Unlike terms cannot be added the way like terms are added means unlike term left as they are.
Example: 3xy + 7.
Addition of General Algebraic Expression:
⇒ Horizontal Steps:
To add the general algebraic expressions, we have to arrange them so that the like terms come together, then simplify the terms, and the unlike terms will remain the same in the resultant expression.
Add them as we add other numbers.
If any term of the same variable is not there in another expression then write is as it is in the solution.
Add: 3x + 11 + 8z and 7x – 5.
The sum = 3x + 11 + 8z + 7x – 5
Rearranging terms = (3x + 7x) + (11 – 5) + 8z = 10x + 6 + 8z

Add them as we add other numbers.

Definition: Equations in Variable Separable Form
The equation \[ rac{dy}{dx} = F(x, y)\] is said to be in
variable separable form
if it can be expressed as \[g(x) dx = h(y) dy\] or equivalently as \[ rac{dy}{dx} = g(x)h(y)\] so that the variables can be separated and integrated.
CBSE: Class 12
Method
Write the equation in the form \[ rac{dy}{dx} = g(x)h(y)\].
Rearrange it so that all y-terms are with dy, and all x-terms are with dx.
\[ rac{1}{h(y)} dy = g(x) dx\]
Integrate both sides.
\[\int  rac{1}{h(y)} dy = \int g(x) dx\]
Add the constant of integration.
\[\int  rac{1}{h(y)} dy = \int g(x) dx + C\]
If an initial condition is given, substitute it to obtain the particular solution.
CBSE: Class 12
Example 1
Solve:
\[ rac{dy}{dx} =  rac{x + 1}{2 - y}\]
Solution:
Separate the variables:
(2 - y) dy = (x + 1) dx
Integrate both sides:
\[\int (2 - y) dy = \int (x + 1) dx\]
\[2y -  rac{y^2}{2} =  rac{x^2}{2} + x + C\]
On simplification, the general solution as
\[x^2 + y^2 + 2x - 4y + C = 0\]
CBSE: Class 12
Key Points: Variable Separable Differential Equations
Variable separable equations can be rewritten as x-part = y-part.
Separate variables first, then integrate.
Use one constant of integration.
Apply the initial condition only after getting the general solution.
Final answers may be explicit or implicit.

CISCE: Class 6
Introduction
Triangle construction is the process of accurately drawing a triangle using basic geometric tools—a ruler (straightedge), a compass, and often a protractor—when given specific measurements. These measurements are typically side lengths or angle measures.
CISCE: Class 6
Construction 1: Three Sides Given (SSS)
Example:
Construct triangle ABC with
AB = 7.6 cm
AC = 6 cm
CB = 4 cm
Steps:
Draw a rough sketch of triangle ABC.
Draw the base AB = 7.6 cm.
With A as center, draw an arc of radius 6 cm.
With B as center, draw another arc of radius 4 cm. Let the arcs intersect at point C.
Join AC and BC.
CISCE: Class 6
Construction 2: Two Sides and Included Angle Given (SAS)
Example:
Construct triangle ABC with
AB = 3 cm
BC = 5 cm
∠ABC = 60°
Steps:
Draw a rough sketch of triangle ABC.
Draw base BC = 5 cm.
At point B, use a protractor to construct ∠ABC = 60°.
With B as the centre, draw an arc of radius 3 cm to locate point A on the 60° line.
Join AC.
CISCE: Class 6
Construction 3: Two Angles and the Included Side Given (ASA)
Example:
Construct triangle ABC with
AB = 4 cm
∠A = 60°
∠B = 30°
Steps:
Draw a rough sketch of triangle ABC.
Draw the base AB = 4 cm.
At point A, draw a 60° angle (ray AP).
At point B, draw a 30° angle (ray BQ).
The point where ray AP and ray BQ meet is point C.
Join AC and BC.
CISCE: Class 6
Key Points Summary
The Three Core Rules:
Triangles are primarily constructed using the three congruence criteria:
SSS
(Side-Side-Side: Three sides given).
SAS
(Side-Angle-Side: Two sides and the included angle given).
ASA
(Angle-Side-Angle: Two angles and the included side given).
Planning First:
Always begin with a
rough sketch
to plan the construction steps and visualize the final shape.
Accuracy is Key:
Use your compass, ruler, and protractor
carefully
to maintain precise measurements throughout the process.

Introduction
The perimeter is the total distance around the outside edge or boundary of any closed two-dimensional shape (a plane figure). If you were to walk along every side of a park and return to your starting point, the total distance you walked would be the perimeter.
Why is it Important?
Understanding perimeter is fundamental in many real-world tasks, such as:
Planning how much fencing is needed for a garden or yard.
Calculating the length of decorative border or trim required for a room.
Measuring the length of a running track or sports field boundary.
